The shoot system includes stems, branches, leaves and flowers. These organs support photosynthesis and reproduction.

The root system consists of roots that anchor the plant, absorb water and mineral salts, and may store food. The shoot system consists of stems, branches, leaves and flowers, and its organs carry out functions such as photosynthesis and reproduction.

Epidermal tissue forms the leaf’s outer protective layer; the cuticle reduces water loss, while stomata regulate gas exchange and water-vapour loss. Mesophyll lies between the epidermal layers, contains chloroplast-rich cells and is the main site of photosynthesis.
Palisade mesophyll consists of tightly packed, elongated cells beneath the upper epidermis. Spongy mesophyll lies below it and has loosely arranged cells with air spaces that aid gas diffusion.

A leaf has epidermal, mesophyll and vascular tissues. Epidermal tissue protects the leaf, and stomata regulate gas exchange and water-vapour loss. Mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, while air spaces in spongy mesophyll aid gas diffusion. Vascular tissue contains xylem, which transports water and minerals to the leaf, and phloem, which transports sugars from the leaf.

Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals, and may store food. Stems support leaves, flowers and fruits and transport water, minerals and nutrients. Leaves are the main sites of photosynthesis and transpiration. Flowers are involved in sexual reproduction.
The root system consists of roots, usually underground, that anchor the plant, absorb water and mineral salts from the soil, and may store food.
